issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessing domestic violence, the trigger pattern is strongly male-linked ('being alone with men') but also includes 'being alone with women' without any corresponding formulation or symptom content explaining why both genders would be equivalently triggering. That broadens the trigger profile in a way that is hard to connect to the rest of the report, which is centered on interpersonal threat from others who might harm him rather than gender-nonspecific social presence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Driving/being a passenger in a vehicle' is difficult to link to the reported trauma and the rest of the profile. No other trigger, threat, or memory item involves transport, accidents, escape, or vehicles, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain not represented elsewhere in the five components.

vignette:
Keanu, an exceptionally bright and driven 18-year-old, presented for therapy describing a life that felt increasingly constricted, as if the walls were closing in on him. Despite his recent promotion to a junior Project Manager role, a position that should have been a source of pride, he reported a pervasive sense of dread that he could no longer manage on his own. The origin of this feeling, he explained, was not a single event but a constellation of memories from his childhood that refused to stay in the past. He doesn't remember all of it, acknowledging that it feels like an "incomplete picture," but the parts he does recall surface not as a narrative but as raw, sensory fragments.

The most vivid of these "disconnected pieces" is from when he was about eight years old. He remembers the sharp, sour smell of beer on his father's breath, a scent that now, when he catches it on a coworker after lunch or on someone passing him on the street, triggers an immediate, cold spike of fear. He recalls the sound of his mother's pleading voice and the sight of his father's face, tight with a rage that seemed to consume him. The memory that haunts him most, however, is the image of his own blue bicycle-a recent birthday present-being lifted and thrown across the living room, its metal frame crashing against the far wall. When he tries to recall what happened next, the memory dissolves, but remembering that moment alone is enough to bring back the same suffocating "terror on recall" he felt as a small, powerless boy.

In the years that followed, Keanu learned to navigate a world he perceived as fundamentally unsafe. He developed a keen, almost painful awareness of other people, constantly "watching others closely for signs that they might harm" him. At his open-plan office, he finds himself tracking the tones of voice and body language of his male colleagues, bracing for an explosion of anger over a missed deadline or a minor disagreement. This fear is most acute when he is alone with men. He has gone to great lengths to "avoid other people" in these situations, fabricating last-minute emergencies to get out of one-on-one meetings with male stakeholders or insisting a female colleague join him, a pattern that has begun to draw quiet notice from his superiors.

His home, which he shares with his girlfriend, offers little respite. He is plagued by a constant sense of vulnerability. Before they can go to sleep, he must perform a meticulous ritual of "repeatedly checking that doors and windows are locked," sometimes getting out of bed two or three times to re-check a lock he knows is secure. Any unexpected noise-a car door slamming on the street, a dish dropped in the kitchen-causes him to "jump or startle," his heart hammering in his chest. To quiet the ceaseless internal alarm, he has come to rely on a chain of maladaptive strategies. He began "smoking" heavily in his mid-teens, and more recently has started to "drink alcohol" most evenings, chasing a numbness that never quite arrives.

It was his girlfriend who finally urged him to seek help. She has grown increasingly worried by his escalating drinking, his exhaustion, and the frantic way he scans every room they enter. The catalyst was a near-miss two weeks ago, when he almost stepped into traffic after seeing a bicycle, identical in color to his childhood one, chained to a post. The sight had momentarily overwhelmed him, a flash of mangled blue metal and the echo of a crash filling his senses. Keanu came to his first session admitting he was terrified. He feels he is losing control, and what frightens him most is the belief that the violent unpredictability he witnessed as a child is a danger that still lurks around every corner, and in every person he meets.
